lesson.title: Charging Against Time: The RC Circuit's Exponential Curve
lesson.summary: Combining a resistor and a capacitor in series produces something neither part shows alone: a voltage that climbs smoothly toward its final value over time, following a curve set entirely by the product of R and C.
lesson.body:
A resistor by itself, governed by Ohm's law, relates voltage and current instantly, at every moment in time. A capacitor by itself stores charge and resists changes to its own voltage. Put the two in series with a voltage source, and a new behavior appears that neither component shows alone: the current and voltage in the circuit now change over time in a smooth, predictable curve, rather than jumping immediately to some fixed value.

The intuition follows directly from the capacitor's nature. At the instant a switch closes, the capacitor is uncharged, so it presents 0 volts, and by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the entire source voltage appears across the resistor, producing the maximum possible current, I0 = V over R, which is just Ohm's law applied to that first instant. As charge builds on the capacitor's plates, its voltage rises, which means the voltage left over across the resistor (the source voltage minus the capacitor's voltage) shrinks, so the current shrinks too, so charging slows further, a classic diminishing returns process. The formal solution to this is Vc(t) = V times (1 minus e to the power of negative t over RC), where the product R times C, called the time constant and written tau, sets the pace of the whole curve, in seconds when R is in ohms and C is in farads.

Worked example: let R = 10 kilohms and C = 100 microfarads, chosen so the numbers stay clean. The time constant is tau = RC = 10000 times 0.0001 = 1 second. Starting from an uncharged capacitor with a 5 volt source, after exactly one time constant, t = 1 second, the capacitor voltage is Vc = 5 times (1 minus e to the negative 1) = 5 times (1 minus 0.3679) = 5 times 0.6321, about 3.16 volts. That 63.2 percent figure is not specific to this example, after exactly one time constant, any RC circuit has always closed 63.2 percent of the gap between its starting voltage and its final voltage, regardless of the specific R and C chosen.

By convention, the capacitor is considered essentially fully charged after about five time constants, over 99 percent of the way there. Discharging works as the mirror image: with the source removed and the capacitor released to discharge through a resistor, Vc(t) = V0 times e to the negative t over RC, decaying smoothly from its starting voltage toward zero using that same time constant.

This exponential charge and discharge behavior underlies a huge range of practical circuits: it sets the timing intervals in oscillators and classic 555 timer circuits, smooths out (filters) noisy DC power supplies, and defines the cutoff frequency of a simple filter through f_c = 1 over (2 pi RC). Choosing a larger R or a larger C always stretches the curve out in time without changing its basic shape, which is exactly why timer circuits are tuned by swapping a resistor or capacitor value rather than redesigning the whole circuit. Together with its mirror image, the RL circuit covered next, it is the fundamental building block for understanding how any circuit responds to a sudden change.
